action: Option B is empirically justified. No rerun needed.

pivot_reasons.1.3: Community-set Jaccard=0.842 > 0.7 — both groups share the same community tier. Within-community rank noise will prevent stable binary separation regardless of propagation probability.
pivot_reasons.2.1: Maximum estimated Jaccard across all thresholds [3%–30%] = 0.657 < 0.7 (feasibility minimum). The IC score distribution has no region with sufficient gap-to-noise ratio for stable binary labeling.

evidence_statement_for_paper:
Empirical analysis of the Twitch EN graph (168,114 nodes; mean degree ≈ 81) under the weighted-cascade IC model (p(u,v) = kappa/degree(v), kappa=1) yields the following diagnostic evidence on binary top-k labeling stability:
• Regime: near-critical-moderate — cv_score=0.2109 (target > 0.3), mean_reach=26.2 nodes (0.0156% of LCC).
• Degree separation (KS) top-10% vs top-11–20%: KS=0.4220 (verdict: separable; pivot threshold: KS < 0.15) — groups are structurally separable, ruling out signal absence as the cause of label instability.
• Community-tier overlap: set-Jaccard=0.842, 84.2% communities span both groups.
• Max estimated Jaccard across all percentile thresholds [3%–30%]: 0.6566 at 30% (feasibility minimum: 0.7).
These are intrinsic properties of the graph topology and propagation regime, not simulation artifacts. Accordingly, we adopt continuous regression on log-transformed IC scores (y = log1p(ic_score_mean)) as the primary evaluation framework (Option B). Binary labels are retained as supplementary only, with explicit uncertainty disclosure (uncertainty_boundary_ratio=19.9%).

option_b_justification.conclusion: Regression target (log1p IC score mean) is substantially more stable than binary top-10% labels. Spearman rank correlation remains consistent while Jaccard collapses — confirming the problem is threshold-cutting noise, not signal absence.
